title: Peripheral Blood Smear Preparation & Staining

references.label: Standard clinical hematology laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management)

purpose: To prepare a thin, evenly distributed blood film on a slide and stain it so red cells, white cells, and platelets can be examined microscopically for morphology and estimated numbers.
principle: A drop of well-mixed anticoagulated (or capillary) blood is spread into a thin monolayer using the wedge technique, air-dried, then stained with a Romanowsky-type stain (e.g. Wright or Wright-Giemsa), which differentially colors nuclear chromatin, cytoplasmic granules, and hemoglobin so cell types and abnormal morphology become visible under the microscope.
requiredMaterials: Clean glass slides (one as the smear slide, one as the spreader slide)
requiredReagents: Romanowsky-type stain (e.g. Wright or Wright-Giemsa stain)
Buffered rinse solution appropriate to the stain

procedure.instruction: Place a small drop of well-mixed blood near one end of a clean slide.

procedure.note: Angle and speed control smear thickness — too steep or too slow makes the smear too thick; too shallow or fast makes it too thin/short.
procedure.instruction: Using a second slide held at roughly a 30–45° angle as the spreader, draw the drop into a thin, feathered-edge film across the slide in one smooth, even motion.
Air-dry the smear completely before staining.

procedure.note: Follow the manufacturer's or laboratory's validated timing for the exact stain product — Romanowsky stain formulations and protocols differ.
procedure.instruction: Fix and stain per the specific Romanowsky stain protocol in use (fixation time, stain time, and buffer/rinse steps vary by product), then rinse and air-dry.

Examine under low power first to assess overall smear quality and cell distribution, then scan the feathered edge and monolayer, and finally examine under oil immersion (1000×) for detailed morphology.

observations: A well-made smear has a gradual feathered edge, an even monolayer region where cells don't overlap, and clear staining differentiation between cell types.
interpretation: The peripheral smear supports/confirms automated CBC findings, flags red cell shape abnormalities (e.g. sickle cells, spherocytes, schistocytes), white cell morphology and left-shift, platelet clumping (which can falsely lower an automated platelet count), and can reveal blood parasites — see the related blood parasite microscopy entry.
precautions: Handle all blood specimens and stained slides as biohazardous.
Use fresh, well-anticoagulated (not clotted or excessively aged) blood for the most representative morphology.
limitations: A poorly made smear (too thick, too thin, or with an uneven feathered edge) can distort apparent cell morphology and counts and should be remade rather than over-interpreted.
Morphologic assessment has inherent inter-observer variability, which QC/proficiency programs are designed to monitor.
biosafetyNotes: Treat all specimens and prepared slides as biohazardous; dispose of slides per sharps/biohazard policy.
